findings.quote: That faster repair genuinely helps, but a cable network only stays resilient as long as no single cable is left carrying too much of the traffic.
findings.note: Same option-cluster tell, form-only: A is an overclaim ('the surest way ... is to cut the mean time to repair'), C a recommendation ('operators should give priority'), D a bare process description. B is the only thesis and the only concessive 'X helps, but only while Y' option. The lone hedged option among absolutes decides a main-idea stem without the passage.

findings.quote: and it would have gone on shortening it without any limit however large the fleet was allowed to grow
findings.note: B is an unbounded absolute and D shifts the axis to fault type rather than to fleet size, so two options fall on form. A vs C (both region types vs only the diversifying ones) is a real contrast the passage must settle.

findings.quote: It fell slowly at first and then stopped falling almost entirely once a single cable carried more than roughly a third of the region's traffic.
findings.note: Extremity gradient plus stem presupposition. The stem singles out 'the regions that added ships but did not spread out their traffic', so A ('staying reassuringly low') and D ('climbed back down over the years') contradict the stem's own framing, and B ('the moment the region first put an extra repair ship to sea') is an absolute. C is the only graded option and the only one with a quantified threshold. Domain knowledge of submarine cables is not used anywhere in that chain.

findings.quote: Because a network can never lose only a little connectivity to a fault unless every single one of its routes is fully duplicated by a second cable laid alongside.
findings.note: B is a blanket 'can never ... unless every single' absolute and C is a generic repair-process fact that does not explain the contrast the stem poses; both fall on form. A remains a substantive confound (calmer waters), so A vs D still needs the passage.

findings.quote: Broadly persuaded: she largely accepts Baumann's rule and treats the concentrating regions' plateau as a minor gap that still-faster mends will close.
findings.note: Redundant-option leak: A ('broadly persuaded ... largely accepts Baumann's rule') and C ('convinced: she shares Baumann's certainty') are the same stance at two intensities and cannot both be the key, so neither is; D is the extreme dismissal. B survives by elimination on form alone, with no knowledge of cable operations used.

findings.quote: That the folding proportion became the common standard less through its own elegance than because one large buyer's cabinet order pushed the trade onto it.
findings.note: The sheet's own later stems ('after the Wenmarch Assurance Office's 1913 order'; 'what actually spread the folding size among ordinary firms once the Assurance Office had adopted it') announce the contingency thesis, so the main-idea item is decided by cross-question corroboration; independently A is absolute ('always bound to be recognised'), B is a definitional aside and D a contrarian detail.

findings.quote: It won the final round by a single vote over a squarer sheet that the printers preferred and that would have cost the trade less to adopt.
findings.note: A ('agreed on it comfortably ... from the very first round of voting onward') contradicts the contingency thesis the sheet's other stems already expose, and q5's option B cites 'the minutes and returns', implying a contested vote on record. B is the hedged specific narrative left standing; C and D remain substantive, so major not lethal.

findings.quote: It climbed sharply: within four years the count of firms on the standard had passed six hundred, up from fewer than thirty a year after the rule.
findings.note: A ('changed little') contradicts the thesis the sheet's other stems establish, C is absolute ('every paper-using firm in the whole trade ... entirely'), and B introduces a compulsory government mandate nothing else in the sheet hints at. The single numerically specific option is the visible key shape blind.

findings.quote: That the Wenmarch Assurance Office had ordered all of its own correspondence to be kept and filed on the folding size.
findings.note: B is circular against its own stem ('once the Assurance Office had adopted it'), so it cannot be the spreading mechanism; D is absolute ('physically incapable of holding any sheet but the folding size ... no other option at all'); C contradicts the sheet's non-merit thesis. That leaves A, reachable without the passage.

findings.quote: In full agreement: she too concludes that a proportion that good needed no lucky customer and would sooner or later have prevailed anywhere on its own.
findings.note: Stance duplication: A ('merely hurried along an outcome the proportion's own merits would have reached in any case') and C assert substantially the same position at different intensities, so neither can be uniquely correct; D is an extreme ('Openly scornful'). B survives on option semantics alone, with no domain knowledge required. Flagged rather than killed because A and C are arguably separable on the 'lucky push' clause.

findings.quote: That a sheet proportion elegant enough to survive folding was always bound to be recognised as the best one and duly written into the rules.
findings.note: 'always bound to be' — teleological absolute, form-only elimination; it is also the position q:5's stem attributes to Ferrowby, i.e. the named foil.

findings.quote: That every size in the paper family is simply the size above it folded in half, which is what makes the folding proportion so convenient to use.
findings.note: True-but-definitional: no thesis, so it cannot be the main idea of a history item. Two eliminations leave C vs D, and q:3/q:4 stems (both presupposing the 1913 order drove uptake) push C without the passage.

findings.quote: It rose steadily until, within a few years, every paper-using firm in the whole trade had gone over entirely to the folding size.
findings.note: 'every ... in the whole trade ... entirely' — universal overreach, discardable on form.

findings.quote: It spread only after the government stepped in and made the folding size compulsory for all official and commercial correspondence.
findings.note: Retired cross-question rather than by form: q:4's stem asserts the Assurance Office's adoption is what spread the size among ordinary firms, which excludes a government mandate and also excludes A ('changed little'), leaving the concrete-figures option D decidable without reading the passage.

findings.quote: That the new filing cabinets were physically incapable of holding any sheet but the folding size, leaving every firm that bought one no other option at all.
findings.note: Absolute twin of A ('physically incapable', 'no other option at all'): same mechanism at implausible strength, so the hedged member of the pair is the form-favoured pick.

findings.quote: That the office publicised the folding proportion's geometric advantages until other firms were persuaded of its merits and chose to switch across.
findings.note: The stem's 'actually spread' signals a non-obvious mechanism and so disfavours persuasion-by-merit. B remains substantive (an office filing rule can pull correspondents along), so the item is not decided — better than chance, not a giveaway.

findings.quote: In full agreement: she too concludes that a proportion that good needed no lucky customer and would sooner or later have prevailed anywhere on its own.
findings.note: Absolute version of A ('needed no lucky customer', 'anywhere on its own') — eliminable by form.

findings.quote: Openly scornful: she regards the folding sheet as a poor choice that a single office ended up forcing on an unwilling and resistant trade.
findings.note: Off-target extreme: the quoted claim is about inevitability, not about the sheet's quality. A and B both survive as substantive authorial stances within the question; only q:1's contrastive main-idea option decides B.
